body.heading: Twelve grapes and first feet
paragraphs: In Spain, the turn of the year is eaten: twelve grapes, one with each midnight chime, for twelve months of luck. In Scotland, “first-footing” sends the first visitor across the threshold with gifts like coal, bread, or whisky — symbols of warmth, food, and cheer for the year ahead. In Denmark, people leap from chairs at midnight, jumping into the new year in the most literal way available.

In Japan, temple bells ring 108 times to clear the desires that trouble the human heart, while in many Chinese celebrations of the Lunar New Year, red envelopes of money pass from elders to children with wishes for prosperity.

body.heading: The wishes underneath
paragraphs: Strip away the costumes and the wishes converge: health, enough food, warmth, luck, a clean start. Cultures that agree on little else agree that a year should begin with hope spoken out loud, in company, preferably with something delicious in hand.
Even the cleaning customs — sweeping out the old year, settling debts, wearing new clothes — tell the same story: beginnings deserve a cleared stage.

body.heading: Borrow one
paragraphs: There is no rule that your household may keep only its own traditions. Eat twelve grapes, leap off a sofa, write wishes on paper to burn or keep — adopted rituals, practised with respect and a little humour, become real ones by repetition.
What matters is the marking. A year that is welcomed deliberately is a year the family remembers choosing.

takeaway: Beneath every new-year custom sits the same wish list: health, warmth, enough, and a clean start.
